Neonatal Seminole bats emerge weighing approximately 3.0 grams [Wwb = approximately 3.0 grams], a birth mass that reflects the species' reliance on stored maternal resources during the initial days of life. This value was estimated based on comparative data from the congeneric hoary bat Lasiurus cinereus, whose larger body size provides a scaling reference for the smaller Seminole bat. At birth, the altricial pups exhibit limited mobility and depend entirely on their mother for thermoregulation and nutrition. The species typically produces two to three pups per litter [N_R_i = two to three pups per litter], with females giving birth to a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year]. Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species, estimated at 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], the gestational period lasts approximately 56 days [tg = approximately 56 days], a duration inferred from reproductive data available for Lasiurus cinereus. This relatively rapid gestation is characteristic of vespertilionid bats and allows parturition to coincide with peak insect abundance in late spring, maximizing neonatal survival.

Following parturition, the nursing period proceeds through a critical developmental window before young achieve nutritional independence. The time since birth at weaning is estimated at 34 days [tx = 34 days] under the same thermal conditions of 34.8 °C, with this value similarly derived from observations of Lasiurus cinereus at a temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. During this suckling stage, which spans approximately five weeks, the milk-dependent pups undergo rapid somatic growth, more than quadrupling their birth mass before they begin consuming solid food. The onset of lactation occurs almost immediately after the birth event, with the dam providing frequent nursing bouts throughout each night. The pre-weaning juvenile remains within the maternal roost, often clinging to the mother's fur during foraging excursions in the early weeks. By the end of the nursing stage, young bats have developed sufficient flight capabilities and foraging skills to begin independent feeding, though they may continue to roost with their mother for several additional weeks.

Sexual maturation in Seminole bats occurs relatively late compared to the short gestation and weaning periods. The time since birth at puberty is 365 days [tp = 365 days] when maintained at a body temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This one-year interval means that individuals born in late spring typically do not attain reproductive maturity until the following breeding season, effectively making them incapable of breeding during their first summer of life. Juveniles undergo gonadal development throughout their first winter, with spermatogenesis in males and follicular development in females progressing gradually. The onset of puberty coincides with the completion of skeletal growth, as sub-adults reach adult body dimensions by approximately eleven months of age. This delayed maturation is ecologically significant, as it ensures that only physiologically robust individuals contribute to the next generation, thereby maintaining population stability in fluctuating prey environments.

Adult female Seminole bats attain a maximum wet weight of 14 grams [Wwi = 14 grams], based on published accounts describing a typical range of 7 to 14 grams in this species. This modest body mass, among the smallest in the genus Lasiurus, influences nearly every aspect of the species' life history, from metabolic rate to reproductive output. At a body temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], the species exhibits a minimum oxygen consumption of 13.50 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 13.50 milliliters of oxygen per hour], representing the peak basal metabolic rate measured under controlled laboratory conditions. This relatively elevated metabolic rate, coupled with the small body size, necessitates frequent feeding bouts throughout the night. The energetic demands of flight, thermoregulation, and lactation impose substantial physiological costs, particularly on reproductive females who must maintain positive energy balance while provisioning their young. Comparative analyses with larger congeners suggest that the Seminole bat's high mass-specific metabolism constrains its geographic distribution to warmer regions where insect biomass remains consistently available.

Maximum longevity in the Seminole bat reaches 5110 days [am = 5110 days] when evaluated at the typical active body temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], a lifespan that equates to approximately 14 years. This extended longevity is noteworthy for a mammal of this small size and contrasts with the relatively short lifespans observed in many similar-sized insectivorous bats from temperate regions. The ability to survive for over a decade reflects a suite of life-history adaptations, including delayed reproduction, low annual fecundity, and efficient energy utilization during winter torpor. Oldest documented individuals from field studies have been recorded at ages exceeding 12 years, suggesting that the physiological limits may approach 15 years under optimal conditions. The species' reliance on stable, warm-weather habitats likely reduces the extrinsic mortality risks associated with harsh winters, allowing more individuals to reach advanced ages. Reproductive senescence has not been well documented in this species, but captive observations suggest that females remain fertile well into their second decade of life, producing one litter annually with consistent pup survival rates.
